Catania
kuh-TAH-nee-uh
n. (the Sicilian city under Etna, rebuilt after the eruption of 1669 and the earthquake of 1693, and seat of the island's oldest university)
From Greek Katane, a Chalcidian colony of 729 before Christ, the name of Sicel origin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Catania lies on the east coast of Sicily beneath Etna and has been destroyed repeatedly: by the lava flow of 1669 which reached the sea through the city, and by the earthquake of 1693 which killed a large part of the population of eastern Sicily. It was rebuilt each time on the same ground, in the baroque that now gives the city its character, and its university, founded in 1434, is the oldest on the island. The dictionary records Catania for the sake of the question a city under a volcano forces. Scripture does not permit the reading of particular disasters as particular verdicts on particular people, and Christ says so explicitly about a tower that fell and a massacre in the temple. It also does not permit the modern move of treating such events as meaningless. They are summons. Catania's people rebuilt under the mountain, which is what men do and is not wrong; the dictionary only insists that a city which has twice been buried has been spoken to, and that the content of the speech is repentance rather than information about the dead.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a volcano as a burning mountain; an earthquake as a shaking of the earth; calamity as any great misfortune; providence as the care of God over his creatures; and repentance as sorrow for sin with amendment.

expand to see more

VOLCANO, n. A burning mountain; a mountain that vomits or has vomited fire, smoke, cinders, ashes and lava.

EARTHQUAKE, n. A shaking, trembling or concussion of the earth; sometimes a slight tremor, at other times a violent shaking.

CALAMITY, n. Any great misfortune or cause of misery; generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evils.

PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a providing or preparing beforehand.

REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, with a sincere purpose of amendment.

Key Scripture

Luk 13:4 — "Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?"

Luk 13:5 — "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."

Amo 4:12 — "Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel."

Psa 46:2 — "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea;"

Modern Corruption

Sicilian city beneath Etna, destroyed by the lava of 1669 and the earthquake of 1693 and rebuilt on the same ground, seat of the island's oldest university.

expand to see more

The corruption to name has two forms and the dictionary rejects both. The first reads a disaster as a judgment on its victims, which Christ forbids by name, asking of eighteen men killed by a falling tower whether they were sinners “above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?” (Luk 13:4). The second treats the event as pure mechanism with no address in it, which is the modern instinct and is equally unavailable, because Christ's own conclusion from the tower is a command to everybody else: “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luk 13:5).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a city under a mountain is in the same position as every other city, only more visibly. Amos states the summons in the form it always takes, “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel” (Amo 4:12), and the psalmist supplies the courage to live there, refusing fear in the exact scenario Catania keeps living through: “Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea” (Psa 46:2). The dictionary honours the Catanesi for rebuilding; it declines to pretend the mountain said nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek metanoeo (G3340), to repent; Hebrew qum (H6965), to arise; Hebrew har (H2022), a mountain.

expand to see more

Greek opheiletes (G3781) — a debtor, and so an offender; “above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem”, Luke 13:4.

Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; “except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish”, Luke 13:5.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to make firm, to prepare; “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel”, Amos 4:12.

Hebrew har (H2022) — a mountain, a hill; “though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea”, Psalm 46:2.

Hebrew yare' (H3372) — to fear, to be afraid; “Therefore will not we fear”, Psalm 46:2.

Usage

"“above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem” (Luk 13:4) — the reading of disaster Christ forbids."

"“except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luk 13:5) — the reading he commands instead."

"“Therefore will not we fear” (Psa 46:2) — the courage to rebuild under the mountain."
